ollama pull bge-m3

Managing the Knowledge Base and Providing a Local Interface with Cherry Studio

After installing Deepseek, although we can interact with Deepseek from the command line, it is still not friendly enough, and managing the local knowledge base is not convenient either. So here we can also install Cherry Studio, an open-source local AI assistant and knowledge base client. Just download the Windows version from the official website (https://cherry-ai.com) and install it.

item.title: How Can Test Developers Make Good Use of Cursor?
item.description:
Preface

Many people who are new to AI-assisted programming have probably heard of how powerful Cursor is. For beginners, the free quota of the free version of Cursor is more than enough to let everyone experience its formidable capabilities.

However, in real-world use — based on my own experience — if you simply treat it as a conversation partner and complete development tasks the way you would communicate with a person, you will waste a great deal of time correcting its misunderstandings, and there is a very high chance that after some conversation it will alter your original work beyond recognition, wasting a large amount of effort.

Cursor’s 12 Rules

In fact, whether Cursor can work more effectively has a lot to do with how you use it. Cursor’s chief designer Ryo Lu earlier shared on X 12 rules for making good use of Cursor:

  1. Set clear project rules: Before starting a project, define 5-10 clear project rules so Cursor understands your code structure and constraints. For existing codebases, you can try the /generate rules command to generate rules.
  2. Be specific in prompts: Be very specific in your prompts, detailing the tech stack, expected behavior, and constraints, just like writing a mini spec.
  3. Work file by file: Handle a small portion each time; generate, test, and review while staying focused.
  4. Tests first: Write tests first, lock down the test cases, then generate code until all tests pass.
  5. Strict review and correction: Always review the AI’s output and manually fix any errors, then tell Cursor to use those corrections as examples.
  6. Limit the scope: Use commands such as @ file, @ folders, and @ git to restrict Cursor’s attention to specific parts of the codebase.
  7. Provide full context: Keep design documents and checklists in the .cursor/ directory so the Cursor agent can fully understand what needs to be done next.
  8. Fix wrong code directly: If the generated code is wrong, just modify it manually. Cursor learns faster from edits than from explanations.
  9. Leverage chat history: Use chat history to iterate on old prompts without starting from scratch.
  10. Choose models wisely: Select models purposefully according to your needs. For example, Gemini suits the pursuit of precision, while Claude suits scenarios requiring broader knowledge.
  11. Handle new or unfamiliar stacks: When working with a new or unfamiliar tech stack, paste in links to the relevant documentation. Have Cursor explain all errors and fixes line by line.
  12. Optimize performance for large projects: For large projects, let it index overnight and limit the context scope to keep performance smooth.

Using Cursor well = fast, clean code.
Using it wrong = AI spaghetti you’ll be cleaning up all week.
Here’s how to actually use it right:
1. Set 5-10 clear project rules upfront so Cursor knows your structure and constraints. Try /generate rules for existing codebases.
2. Be specific in prompts. Spell out tech stack, behavior, and constraints like a mini spec.
3. Work file by file; generate, test, and review in small, focused chunks.
4. Write tests first, lock them, and generate code until all tests pass.
5. Always review AI output and hard‑fix anything that breaks, then tell Cursor to use them as examples.
6. Use @ file, @ folders, @ git to scope Cursor’s attention to the right parts of your codebase.
7. Keep design docs and checklists in .cursor/ so the agent has full context on what to do next.
8. If code is wrong, just write it yourself. Cursor learns faster from edits than explanations.
9. Use chat history to iterate on old prompts without starting over.
10. Choose models intentionally. Gemini for precision, Claude for breadth.
11. In new or unfamiliar stacks, paste in link to documentation. Make Cursor explain all errors and fixes line by line.
12.Let big projects index overnight and limit context scope to keep performance snappy.
Structure and control wins (for now)
Treat Cursor agent like a powerful junior — it can go far, fast, if you show it the way.

How Can Test Developers Make Good Use of Cursor?

As a test developer or test automation engineer, how can we make good use of Cursor when writing test scripts or tools to better improve our efficiency and output? In this article, referring to the 12 rules above, we summarize a set of relevant practical guidelines.

Initialization and Context Building - Training Cursor into a “Test Domain Expert”

At the start of a project or when joining it midway, the first priority is to let Cursor fully understand the standards and constraints of the current testing environment. High-quality context input is the prerequisite for high-quality code output.

Define Project Testing Rules and Conventions (Rule 1)

In test automation projects, consistency in coding standards, framework selection, and design patterns is crucial. Based on Rule 1: Set clear project rules, we can use the .cursor/rules.md file to make this tacit team knowledge explicit and provide Cursor with a clear program of action. For existing projects, you can first use the /generate rules command to initially extract the rules, and then add to them manually.

Practical example: In a Python Flask-based web project, the testing stack is Pytest and Selenium. You can define the following rules in .cursor/rules.md:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

# .cursor/rules.md
- [cite_start]All unit test files are named `test_*.py`
- UI test files are named `ui_test_*.py`
- [cite_start]Test functions must start with `test_`
- [cite_start]Use Pytest fixtures for test environment setup and teardown
- [cite_start]UI tests follow the Page Object pattern, with page objects encapsulated
- [cite_start]Avoid hard-coded waits; prefer WebDriver's explicit wait mechanism
- [cite_start]Test reports are generated uniformly with the Allure framework

Provide Detailed Instructions to Simulate “Test Scenarios” (Rule 2)

The quality of your interaction with AI directly determines the quality of the output code. Instructions for test automation especially demand precision, because they must fully describe the feature under test, input data, expected behavior, and even exceptional paths.

Practical example: Write integration tests for the user login feature.

  • Ineffective instruction: Write a login test.
  • Well-structured instruction:
1
2
3
4

Please use the Pytest framework to write integration tests for the user login feature of a Flask application (endpoint POST /api/login, accepting username and password). The following three scenarios need to be covered:
1. Successful login (using admin/password123);
2. Incorrect password (using admin/wrongpass);
3. User does not exist (using nonexistent/anypass). For the success scenario, assert that the HTTP status code is 200 and the response contains a non-empty token. For the failure scenarios, assert that the status code is 401.

Iterative Development and Correction - Achieving “Continuous Integration of Test Code”

Breaking down complex testing tasks and developing through an agile loop of “generate - verify - correct” is an effective strategy for ensuring code quality and project progress.

Small Steps, Incremental Verification (Rule 3)

You should resist the temptation to generate all the tests for an entire complex module in one go.

The right approach is to break the task down into the smallest verifiable units and tackle them one by one.

For example, when writing tests for a set of RESTful APIs, you should follow the logical order of “create user -> get user -> update user -> delete user”, generating and verifying the test code one at a time

This approach helps locate problems quickly and avoids the accumulation of errors.

Applying Test-Driven Development (TDD) (Rule 4)

Test-driven development is a classic model for ensuring code quality, and Cursor can be a powerful accelerator for it. Engineers first define the expected behavior of a function (that is, write the test cases), then have the AI generate implementation code that satisfies those tests.

Practical example: Implement a discount calculation function calculate_discount(price, discount_rate).

  1. Define the test: First ask Cursor: Generate a Pytest test case for the calculate_discount function. When price=100 and discount_rate=0.1, the expected return value is 90; when discount_rate is negative, a ValueError exception should be raised.
  2. Generate the implementation: After the test code test_calculate_discount.py is generated, run it (it will fail at this point), then give Cursor a new instruction: Based on the test cases just generated, implement the calculate_discount function.
  3. Close the verification loop: Once Cursor generates the function implementation, run the tests again until they all pass.

Proactive Correction and Mutual Learning (Rule 5)

It is worth noting that AI-generated code is not always correct, and the engineer’s review and correction is the last line of defense. Fixing errors directly in the code is the most effective way to train Cursor, far better than explaining to it in natural language.

Practical example: For example, in a UI test generated by Cursor, it used an unstable and incorrect XPath locator //button[@id='submit']. After the test run fails, we can directly change it manually to a correct locator, such as //input[@value='Login']. After the correction, you can leave a note in the chat to reinforce its learning: "I have fixed the locator for the login button; the new locator is more accurate. Please refer to this pattern in subsequent tasks." .

Fine-Grained Management - Achieving “Intelligent Scheduling of Test Resources”

In large projects, how to keep Cursor focused on the right information is key to determining its efficiency and relevance.

Precisely Limit the Context Scope (Rule 6)

In a large codebase, testing tasks are often related only to a specific module or service. By using the @folders or @file commands, you can significantly narrow Cursor’s analysis scope and keep it focused on the necessary context.

Practical example: When writing API tests for the user_service microservice, all relevant code resides in the services/user_service/ directory. In this case, you should first enter @folders services/user_service/ before asking, and then describe the specific testing requirements.

Accumulate Project Knowledge to Support Decisions (Rule 7)

You can distill key information such as testing strategy, UI locator priorities, and data mocking conventions into documents stored in the .cursor/ directory. This is equivalent to providing Cursor with a “project-level knowledge base”.

Practical example: Create a .cursor/ui_locators_priority.md file with the content: “UI element locator priority order: ID > Name > CSS Selector > XPath”. You can then reference it when asking: Please refer to the strategy in .cursor/ui_locators_priority.md and generate Selenium locator code for the 'Submit' button on the registration page..

Problem Solving and Efficiency Optimization - Becoming a “Test Efficiency Accelerator”

Mastering advanced usage can further transform Cursor from an everyday assistant into a powerful tool for solving complex problems and accelerating learning.

Choose AI Models Wisely (Rule 10)

Different AI models have different strengths. Choosing the right model based on the characteristics of the testing task can get you twice the result with half the effort.

  • Gemini (precision first): suited to generating unit tests with strict syntax requirements, algorithm validation, or fine-grained test code using specific frameworks (such as React Testing Library).
  • Claude (breadth first): better suited to scenarios that require understanding large amounts of context, such as generating comprehensive integration tests from API documentation, designing end-to-end (E2E) test scenarios, or exploring and suggesting test points in an unfamiliar codebase.

Use Documentation to Quickly Master New Technologies (Rule 11)

When a team introduces a new testing framework (such as Playwright), engineers can use Cursor to quickly get over the learning curve.

Practical example: Provide Cursor directly with a link to the official Playwright documentation and ask it to generate example code. When the generated code throws an error at runtime, you can paste the error message and ask: “This is an error that occurred while running a Playwright script; please explain the cause of the error line by line based on the official documentation and provide suggestions for fixing it.”.

Limit the Context Scope (Rule 12)

When the project codebase is large, index it overnight and limit the context scope.

Practical example:

When working on a large testing project, allow Cursor to handle indexing in the background and do the actual code generation the next day, so as to keep performance smooth.

1
2
3
4

# Prioritize indexing core modules
@folder tests/unit
# Defer loading integration tests
@defer tests/integration

Conclusion

For our actual work, the essence of successfully using Cursor is a process of shifting from an “instruction giver” to an “intelligent collaborator” and a “knowledge guide”. The emphasis is on highlighting its systematic role in intelligent collaboration, knowledge accumulation, and efficiency improvement.

Previously we introduced generating automated test code with AI, as well as controlling a browser through an mcp server, using the AI programming IDE Cursor. With its powerful intelligent analysis and assisted-programming capabilities, Cursor can automatically complete the code implementation for us when we describe a programming requirement in natural language; it is efficient and works very well. But Cursor is not free software; once the trial period ends, using it as a daily tool is still rather expensive.

item.title: The Definitive Guide to Prompt Engineering - The Art and Science of Empowering Software Testing
item.description:
As the wave of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) sweeps across the globe, the field of software testing is undergoing a profound transformation. Traditional testing methods are merging with cutting-edge AI technologies, and Prompt Engineering is precisely the core skill for steering this transformation. This guide delves into the theory, practice, and advanced techniques of prompt engineering, and offers a series of concrete examples tailored to software testing roles, aiming to help test engineers and teams effectively leverage AI to improve testing efficiency, coverage, and depth.

Chapter 1 - Getting to Know Prompt Engineering, the Art of Efficient Dialogue with AI

1.1 What Is Prompt Engineering?

Prompt engineering is a discipline devoted to designing, constructing, and optimizing input text (that is, “prompts”) so as to guide large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 and Claude to generate the high-quality, relevant outputs we expect. If an LLM is a powerful engine packed with vast knowledge, then the prompt is the steering wheel and accelerator that control that engine.

For software testing, prompt engineering is far more than simply “asking AI a question”; it is a strategic form of communication. With carefully designed prompts, testers can drive AI to complete a range of complex testing tasks, such as:

  • Generating test cases: Based on requirements documents, user stories, or code snippets, automatically create functional, boundary, exception, and other types of test cases.
  • Creating test data: Generate diverse test data that conforms to specific formats and business rules.
  • Writing automation scripts: Assist in writing, or directly generate, automation test scripts for frameworks such as Selenium, Cypress, and Playwright.
  • Analyzing test results: Summarize, classify, and perform root cause analysis on large volumes of test logs and reports.
  • Simulating user behavior: Create interaction scenarios that match specific user personas, for User Acceptance Testing (UAT) or exploratory testing.

Mastering prompt engineering means test engineers can hand tedious, repetitive work over to AI, freeing them to devote more energy to more creative and strategic testing activities.

1.2 Core Principles - Clarity, Specificity, and Context

Successful prompt engineering follows one core principle: Garbage In, Garbage Out (GIGO). The quality of the information you give AI directly determines the quality of its output. Therefore, a good prompt typically has the following characteristics:

  • Clear & Specific: Avoid vague, general language. Tell AI directly what you want.
  • Contextual: Provide AI with ample background information, such as descriptions of the feature under test, relevant code, user personas, and business rules.
  • Role Assignment: Have AI play a specific role—for example, “You are a senior software testing expert”—which helps the model respond from a more professional perspective and tone.
  • Format Specification: Clearly define the output format you want, such as JSON, CSV, Markdown tables, or bulleted lists.
  • Iterative Refinement: Few prompts are perfect on the first try. Be prepared to make multiple attempts and adjustments based on AI’s feedback.

Chapter 2 - A Glossary of Prompt Engineering Terminology

To better understand and apply prompt engineering, it is essential to be familiar with the following key terms.
Term Chinese Explanation Description
Prompt Prompt The input text a user provides to an LLM to guide its response.
Zero-shot Prompting Zero-shot prompting Directly asking the LLM to complete a task without providing any examples. Suitable for tasks the model has already mastered.
Few-shot Prompting Few-shot prompting Providing a small number (usually 1-5) of examples in the prompt to show the LLM the expected input-output format and style.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Prompting Chain-of-thought prompting Guiding the LLM to reason step by step before giving the final answer, triggered by phrases such as “Let’s think step by step”.
Role Prompting / Persona Role prompting / persona Assigning the LLM a specific role or identity (such as “senior security test engineer”) to influence the style, tone, and professional depth of its responses.
Context Window Context window The amount of information (measured in tokens) an LLM can remember and process in a single conversation. Information beyond this window is forgotten.
Token Token The basic unit of text an LLM processes, which may be a word, a character, or a word root.
Hallucination Hallucination The phenomenon where an LLM generates information that seems plausible but is actually false or inconsistent with the facts.
Temperature Temperature parameter A parameter controlling output randomness (usually between 0 and 1). A lower temperature makes output more deterministic and consistent, while a higher one makes it more creative and diverse.
Self-Consistency Self-consistency An advanced technique that generates multiple times (using a higher temperature) and “votes” on the results to select the most consistent answer, improving accuracy on complex reasoning tasks.
ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) Reasoning and acting An advanced framework that lets an LLM not only reason but also perform certain “actions” (such as calling external APIs or executing code) and fold the results of those actions into the next step of reasoning.
Delimiter Delimiter Using special characters or tags (such as ```, ###, <tag>) to clearly separate different parts of a prompt (such as instructions, context, and examples).

item.title: A Prompt-Writing Framework for Test Engineers to Use Large AI Models Effectively
item.description:
Preface

With the widespread application of large AI models in software testing, prompt engineering has become a key skill for test engineers to improve efficiency. Through precise prompt design, we can quickly generate test cases, optimize test scenarios, generate automation scripts, and even achieve intelligent test coverage.

So how can we use large models more effectively and have them help us reach the desired results more efficiently? Good prompts let us achieve twice the result with half the effort. The following summarizes, for test engineers, how to write a good prompt framework.

Breaking Down Complex Requirements and Describing Problems Precisely

The effectiveness of large AI models depends heavily on the clarity of the input prompt, that is, on minimizing ambiguity as much as possible. So when entering a prompt, you should break complex tasks down into concrete requirements as much as possible, for example:

  • Scenario-based descriptions: specify the test objective (e.g., “generate boundary-value test cases for the login function”) rather than a vague instruction (e.g., “help me write test cases”).
  • Constraints: add format requirements (e.g., “output in table form”), priorities (e.g., “include only high-risk scenarios”), or technical limitations (e.g., “no third-party APIs involved”).
  • Example guidance: provide sample data or templates to help the model understand the expected output structure.

Using a Structured Framework to Improve Output Stability

By defining a structured prompt framework, you can constrain model behavior and reduce random interference:

  1. Role setting: specify a professional role for the model to play (e.g., “you are a senior testing expert skilled at designing high-coverage test scenarios”).
  2. Step-by-step instructions: break a complex task into multiple steps (e.g., “Step 1: analyze the requirements document; Step 2: identify critical paths; Step 3: generate cases”).
  3. Chain-of-Thought: although many models now offer deep-thinking capabilities, guiding the model’s analysis through prompts can simplify the direction of its reasoning. For example, “first analyze the user operation flow, then focus on generating test cases for exception scenarios”.

Progressive Iterative Optimization and Continuous Prompt Improvement

Large models usually retain conversation context; for the result of each round of feedback, you should keep correcting and gradually move toward the best output.

  • Feedback correction: promptly point out errors in the model’s output (e.g., “case 2 does not cover the timeout scenario, please add it”) and ask for regeneration.
  • Parameter tuning: control output length (e.g., “describe in 50 characters or less”) and the Temperature coefficient to balance the model’s creativity and accuracy.
  • Cross-comparison: there are many open large models today with varying capabilities, and their analysis results can differ considerably. Judge comprehensively and extract the best result.

item.title: The Hidden Concerns Behind the MCP Boom
item.description:
Over the past few weeks, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) has rapidly emerged as the de facto standard for connecting third-party data and tools to LLM-based conversational systems. In a short time, the internet has been flooded with all kinds of flashy application cases, and the room for imagination is enormous. Yet behind this protocol there also lurk some subtle security risks and functional limitations.

Background

The essence of MCP is to act as a bridge for building an “intelligent assistant plugin ecosystem”, allowing users to provide local extension capabilities to various large models and AI clients that support the MCP protocol, so that these LLM-based intelligent interfaces can perform non-text operations through MCP’s “tool calls”. The MCP protocol in effect standardizes the way LLMs interface with local data and tools.

For example, in the previous article, we simply told the large model in Cursor: “Visit the www.saucedemo.com website, log in with problem_user, verify the complete workflow of the site, and record any issues found” , and Cursor then used the playwright-mcp MCP server to call the playwright framework to carry out a series of activities such as launching the browser, visiting, browsing, testing, and recording issues—completing testing activities similar to those of a manual test engineer

So through MCP, its core value is that it breaks through the original role of large AI models as text-based advisory assistants and turns them into actual executors, better able to directly operate local tools and data, providing large models with a universal socket.

The Potential Hidden Concerns

But while we recognize MCP’s enormous potential, we must also see that MCP, as a foundational protocol that has only recently gotten started, is far from perfect, and there are still the following hidden concerns:

Hidden Concern 1 - Security of the Protocol Itself

Authentication Mechanisms

The initial version of MCP did not define an authentication specification, leaving each MCP server to do as it pleased—from cumbersome verification to sensitive data being left completely exposed, a veritable chaos. Although authentication schemes were introduced later, their implementation complexity has sparked new controversy.

The Risk of Local Malicious Code Execution

The protocol supports running MCP servers via standard input/output, which, while lowering the barrier to use, also provides a breeding ground for the spread of malicious code. If a non-technical user runs third-party malicious MCP code and causes a local device security failure, this has become a new attack vector.

MCP’s Trust in User Input

Many MCP servers directly execute user input instructions. When user intent is translated by the LLM and takes effect on the system, traditional security models face a severe challenge: the boundary between user input instructions and attacks on the system is no longer clear.

Hidden Concern 2 - Limitations in Interaction Design

The MCP protocol is oriented more toward LLM interaction, but for users, the interaction is hardly easy to use or friendly.

The Lack of Risk Grading for Different Levels of Operations

Many assistant tools provide a global operation-confirmation mechanism, but the “auto-confirm” habit formed around many harmless tools often leads to serious misoperations, such as the deletion of important local files or sending emails by mistake.

Cost Control Capability

Unlike traditional protocols, in LLM scenarios different volumes of returned tokens incur varying costs, and the cost of serving users depends heavily on the token efficiency of MCP tools, yet the current protocol has no limit on return length to strengthen cost control.

Sacrificing the Advantages of Structured Data

To accommodate LLM preferences, MCP tends to adopt human-readable formats such as plain text / images / audio clips for transmission, sacrificing the advantages of structured data. For services such as maps or Didi-style ride-hailing, which need to ensure location accuracy, trip-detail feedback, and real-time status updates, the current protocol is hardly up to the task. Solving such problems for now still requires some workaround designs at the tool layer.

Hidden Concern 3 - LLM Security

The discussion around the security of large models themselves is still unresolved, and introducing MCP to connect more data and tools makes this problem even more prominent.

MCP Makes Prompt Injection More Powerful

LLMs usually have two layers of instructions: system-level prompts (which control the assistant’s behavior and policies) and user-level prompts (provided by the user). Usually, when prompt injection was mentioned in the past, it referred to malicious user input. A fairly significant vulnerability of the MCP model is that it allows tools provided by third parties to be trusted as part of the assistant’s system-level prompt, thereby granting them greater privileges to override the agent’s behavior.

Sensitive Data Leakage

Beyond malicious hijacking via malicious tools, MCP can also cause users to leak sensitive data unintentionally. Even if a user strictly confirms every operation, data may still be exfiltrated in a “reasonable” way. For example, with your instruction: “Explain my personal medical records to me”, the assistant may launch a medical-retrieval multi-tenant MCP tool and leak your private personal information to the service provider.

MCP servers can also easily hijack or alter user intent through disguised prompts and their actual tool implementations.

Hidden Concern 4 - Breaking Traditional Enterprise Data Access Controls

Unlike the direct leakage of sensitive data, after an enterprise connects large amounts of internal data to an LLM via MCP, ordinary employees may be able to access or infer data they are not authorized to access.

For example, if all of an enterprise’s internal documents are connected to an LLM, an employee, through the assistant:

“Based on all the documents I have permission to access and the company’s appointment and removal notices, infer major events that have not yet been announced, such as layoffs”

Or someone at the manager level:

“I saw an anonymous negative comment about XXX on the internal wiki, the content is XXXX; please analyze the speaking records of members in the XX team and infer who most likely wrote this comment”

Hidden Concern 5 - The Inherent Capability Limits of LLMs

For large-scale MCP integration, the load capacity of the LLM itself may well be unable to cope. Google’s A2A protocol (Agent to Agent) may be a solution, but that is another matter.

MCP’s Effectiveness Depends on the LLM Integrated into the Assistant

One fact is that it is not the case that the more tools and the more data, the more accurate the results; on the contrary, the more similar data and tools there are, the worse the precision of the final output becomes. As the number of MCP servers grows and more tools are integrated, the performance of AI assistants will also decline significantly, and the cost of requests and analysis will increase.

The Gap Between Tool Implementation and User Expectations

In implementation, many MCP servers are essentially functions or methods written to call tools that already exist locally, so their capabilities are mainly constrained by those functions and methods. If users have little understanding of the specific function implementations and simply interact with the LLM following ordinary human communication patterns, they are likely to struggle to get satisfactory results.

“Please find for me all recent blog articles related to AI testing”; this instruction actually requires the local MCP server to have the ability to full-text search local text content, but if the integrated MCP server only includes file-finding functionality, naturally no corresponding results can be obtained.

Conclusion and Outlook

The birth of MCP answers the data-integration needs of the AI era, and its everyday application value is beyond doubt. But we also need a sober awareness: the MCP protocol is still in its growth phase, and while we embrace its applications, we must also recognize the risks within it; combining LLMs with data amplifies existing risks and gives rise to new types of threats.

Most of the views in this article are drawn from Shrivu’s blog (Read the original article)

item.title: Google Launches the A2A Protocol
item.description:
On April 9, Google made a major release of the A2A (Agent to Agent) protocol, adding more fuel to the opening-up and standardization of AI Agent capabilities. So what exactly does this A2A protocol do? What is its relationship with the previously red-hot MCP Server? Will it give rise to a standards war? In this article, let’s get to know this freshly baked A2A protocol and its application scenarios.

A2A and MCP

A2A, namely the Agent to Agent protocol, is an open-source foundational AI protocol just launched by Google, aimed at enabling communication and interoperability between AI Agents. By providing agents with a standardized way to collaborate — that is, regardless of their underlying framework or vendor — different AI Agents can securely exchange information and collaborate, and can work across a variety of enterprise platforms and applications.

This protocol provides a common communication standard between Agent and Agent.

It and the recently red-hot MCP (Model Context Protocol) (introduced in the previous article 【】) are actually not in a competitive relationship. Google’s official release statement also emphasized that this protocol is in fact a complement to the MCP protocol.

MCP is an open protocol launched late last year by the AI company Anthropic (the parent company of Claude), aimed at standardizing the interaction interface between large language models (LLMs) and external data sources and tools.

As mainstream large models such as OpenAI announce support for MCP integration, MCP currently has great potential to become a foundational specification in the AI application field; the recent proliferation of all kinds of MCP Servers springing up like mushrooms after rain also proves that this protocol has gained wide recognition.

As the saying goes, third-rate companies make products, second-rate companies make brands, first-rate companies make standards; Google has keenly captured a very important piece of the puzzle in the AI Agent application standards beyond MCP.

That is, MCP defines the connection between LLMs and Agents, and can use Agents to extend LLM capabilities. In the future there will surely also be Agent stores similar to the App Store, integrating all kinds of different Agents.

But for subsequent large-scale AI applications, many Agents will be integrated to collaborate together, and the interaction between these Agents is precisely the missing piece of the puzzle at present. This is the role A2A plays — very similar to the inter-service communication protocol in a microservices system.

A2A’s Design Principles

The official side has given the design principles of the A2A protocol:

  • Embrace agentic capabilities — A2A is committed to enabling agents to collaborate in natural, unstructured modes, even when they do not share memory, tools, and context. We are enabling truly multi-agent scenarios, rather than confining agents to being a single “tool”.

  • Built on existing standards — the protocol is built on top of existing popular standards, including HTTP, SSE, and JSON-RPC, which means it is easier to integrate with the existing IT stacks that enterprises use every day.

  • Secure by default — A2A is designed to support enterprise-grade authentication and authorization, matching OpenAPI’s authentication schemes at launch.

  • Support for long-running tasks — A2A was designed with flexibility in mind and supports a variety of scenarios, enabling it to excel at a wide range of tasks, from quick tasks to deep research that may take hours or even days (if humans are involved). Along the way, A2A can provide users with real-time feedback, notifications, and status updates.

  • Modality agnostic — the world of agents is not limited to text, which is why we designed A2A to support a variety of modalities, including audio and video streaming.

Main Features

  • Capability discovery — agents can advertise their capabilities using a JSON-format “Agent Card”, allowing client agents to identify the best agent able to perform a task and use A2A to communicate with remote agents.

  • Task management — communication between client and remote agents is oriented toward task completion, with the agent responsible for executing the end user’s request. This “task” object is defined by the protocol and has a lifecycle. It can be completed immediately, or, for long-running tasks, each agent can communicate to stay in sync with one another about the task’s latest completion status. The output of a task is called an “artifact”.

  • Collaboration — agents can send messages to one another to convey context, replies, artifacts, or user instructions.

  • User experience negotiation — each message contains “parts”, that is, fully formed content fragments such as a generated image. Each part has a specified content type, allowing the client and remote agents to negotiate the correct format needed, and explicitly including negotiation of user UI capabilities (such as iframe, video, Web forms, and so on).

The relationship between A2A, MCP, and LLMs:

Protocol Specification

The protocol is currently open source on GitHub, mainly a format specification file in json schema form (for an introduction to json schema, see 【】); the concrete definitions can be found in the source document.

Here is an explanation of the main parts it contains and their roles:

1. AgentAuthentication

This part defines the supported authentication methods, such as OAuth or API keys.

2. AgentCapabilities

Used to identify the scope of an Agent’s capabilities, such as whether it supports real-time communication.

3. AgentCard

Provides an Agent’s core information, such as its functions and skills, to facilitate discovery.

4. AgentProvider

Identifies the organization or company information of the provider.

5. AgentSkill

Describes an Agent’s skills, such as the tasks or functions it can perform.

6. Error Definitions

Contains some predefined Errors — PushNotificationNotSupportedError, InvalidParamsError, and JSONParseError indicate error types such as notifications not supported, invalid parameters, and JSON parsing, respectively.

7. FileContent & FilePart

Used to pass file-related data, such as upload or download operations.

Case Study

a2aprotocol.net provides a case-scenario description of A2A and MCP collaboration.

For applications in the testing field, as in the article 【】, some readers mentioned richer scenarios: integrating test-case parsing, Playwright execution, and issue collection and reporting. This can be accomplished by different Agents, respectively responsible for test-case generation, Playwright execution, and submissions to tools such as ZenTao and Jira. Here, besides the workflow between Agents, the transfer of items like test cases and Bugs between different Agents can be implemented using the A2A protocol.

Relevant practices still await the enrichment of the related Agents; this account will continue to follow up going forward!

Preface

MCP protocol is an open protocol for AI capabilities launched in November 2024 by the AI company Anthropic (the parent company of Claude), aimed at standardizing the interaction interface between large language models (LLMs) and external data sources and tools. Its core design goals:

  • Decoupling and standardization — shifting the integration of LLMs with external systems from custom development to universal connections based on a unified protocol, similar to the USB-C interface in hardware.
  • Decentralization — by allowing developers to build their own MCP Servers, distributing AI capabilities and avoiding a single vendor’s monopoly on knowledge and services.
  • Security and control — ensuring data privacy and operational safety through permission verification and localized deployment.

And MCP Server is the key component of MCP, providing the following three functions:

  • Resources — file-like data that can be read by clients, such as API responses or file contents.
  • Tools — functions that can be called by the LLM (requiring user approval).
  • Prompts — pre-written templates that help users accomplish specific tasks.

Through these capabilities, MCP Server can provide AI applications with richer context and the ability to operate on private data or specific applications, thereby enhancing the usefulness of LLMs.

In the previous article 【】, we gained a basic understanding of MCP Server, provided a basic example of querying the local desktop, and used the AI editor Cursor to invoke this MCP server.

Microsoft Officially Releases Playwright-mcp

Among the many current applications of MCP Server, orchestrating browser operations is an extremely high-frequency scenario. Based on Playwright, this rising new browser tool, third parties have already taken the lead in releasing an MCP Server.

And now, Microsoft has finally officially released Playwright-mcp, which can be used seamlessly with VS Code Copilot.

item.title: The Next Stop for AI - MCP Server
item.description:
Introduction

In 2025, as AI technology evolves at breakneck speed, the limitations of large models are becoming increasingly apparent; they possess powerful reasoning capabilities, yet struggle to directly access private data or invoke external tools. This pain point has given rise to a revolutionary technology — MCP (Model Context Protocol) — and MCP Server, its core component, is fast becoming the next big thing in the AI industry. This article takes a deep dive into the technical essence and industry value of MCP Server, and explores its application prospects through real-world cases.

Part One - What Is MCP? The Past and Present of MCP

1. The Definition and Design Goals of MCP

MCP is an open protocol introduced by the AI company Anthropic (the parent company of Claude) in November 2024, designed to standardize the interaction interface between large language models (LLMs) and external data sources and tools. Its core design goals:

  • Decoupling and Standardization: Transforming the integration of LLMs with external systems from custom development into universal connections based on a unified protocol, similar to the USB-C interface in hardware.
  • Decentralization: By allowing developers to build their own MCP Servers, AI capabilities are distributed, preventing a single vendor from monopolizing knowledge and services.
  • Security and Control: Ensuring data privacy and operational safety through permission verification and local deployment.

2. The Technical Evolution from Langchain to MCP

Before MCP, developers relied on middleware frameworks such as Langchain to connect LLMs with tools, but these solutions had two major bottlenecks:

  1. Fragmentation: API standards vary across vendors, making integration costly;
  2. Closedness: The plugin ecosystems of vendors such as OpenAI are confined to their own platforms, making reuse across models difficult.

Through abstraction at the protocol layer, MCP encapsulates capabilities such as tool invocation and data access into standardized interfaces, so that any LLM supporting the MCP protocol can seamlessly connect to third-party services.

3. The Current State of the MCP Ecosystem

At this stage, the MCP ecosystem has begun to take shape:

  • Support from Leading Companies: Besides Claude from the company that initiated it, OpenAI, a leader in the AI industry, as well as domestic players such as Baidu and Tencent, have all announced support for MCP
  • A Large Developer Base: Thanks to a low barrier to entry, the various publicly available MCP Servers have grown explosively; within just a few weeks, thousands of public Servers have appeared, covering areas such as databases, design tools, and payment systems.
  • Emerging Business Value: Institutions such as a16z have drawn up MCP market maps, predicting it may give rise to a “Stripe of the Agentic AI space” caliber company.

Part Two - What Does MCP Server Do? Why Might It Be the AI Industry’s Next Big Thing?

1. The Core Functions of MCP Server

An MCP Server is a concrete implementation of the MCP protocol, playing the following key roles:

  • Tool Proxy: Converting external APIs (such as GitHub and PostgreSQL) into standardized tool descriptions that LLMs can understand, for example abstracting “create a GitHub Issue” into a function call.
  • Data Gateway: Securely accessing local or cloud data, for example letting an LLM read desktop files through a file-system MCP Server.
  • Workflow Orchestration: Supporting chained calls across multiple tools, for example querying a database first and then generating a report.

2. Three Major Drivers Behind the Craze

(1) Technology Trend - From “Fat Models” to “Thin Models + Ecosystem”

Traditional “fat models” try to internalize all knowledge within their parameters, resulting in high training costs and poor timeliness. Under the MCP architecture, LLMs focus on language understanding, while knowledge extension and tool invocation are handled by the MCP Server network, forming a new paradigm of “thin models + distributed capabilities”.

(2) Economic Model - The AI-ification of the Creator Economy

MCP allows individual developers to earn revenue shares by building MCP Servers (such as a bird knowledge base), forming a decentralized knowledge economy network. For example, OpenMCP.Network, built on Ethereum, can automatically settle call volumes through smart contracts.

(3) Industry Demand - The Rigid Need for Private Enterprise AI Deployment

Enterprises can use MCP Servers to securely expose internal systems (such as CRM and ERP) to LLMs without uploading sensitive data to the cloud. Companies such as NineData have launched database MCP Server solutions that support localized data management.

Part Three - As Software Testing Professionals, How Do We Apply MCP Server?

1. MCP-ifying Testing Scenarios

(1) Simulating External Dependencies

By building Mock MCP Servers to replace dependencies such as real payment and third-party APIs, test environment isolation is achieved. For example, simulating the Alipay interface returning an abnormal response to verify the system’s fault tolerance.

(2) Data-Driven Testing

Store test cases in a database or file, and have the MCP Server read and execute them dynamically. For example:

The test framework can automatically obtain the cases and generate test reports.

(3) AI-Assisted Testing

Use LLMs to invoke testing tools through MCP Servers, for example:

  • Automatic Test Script Generation: Generating Selenium code from requirement descriptions;
  • Intelligent Log Analysis: Locating the root causes of defects with an ELK Stack MCP Server.

2. Skill Upgrade Suggestions for Testing Professionals

  • Master MCP Server Development: Learn the Python/TypeScript MCP SDKs to build customized testing tools.
  • Get Familiar with the Mainstream MCP Ecosystem: Follow the Awesome MCP Servers list on GitHub to learn about testing-related services (such as PostgreSQL and JIRA integrations).

Part Four - A Simple MCP Server Implementation Case - A Desktop File Query Service

Conclusion

MCP Server is reshaping the way AI interacts with the physical world. For developers, it is a sharp tool for lowering integration costs; for enterprises, it is the key to unlocking the value of data; for testing professionals, it is a new engine for the evolution of automation. Although the ecosystem is still in its early days, its standardized, decentralized design philosophy has already pointed the way to the next stop for the AI industry. As Anthropic put it, “MCP is not the destination, but the starting point of the Agentic AI era.”

item.title: Software Testing in the AI Era - Assistant or Adversary?
item.description:
In the present era, the AI wave is sweeping in, and “the future is already here” is no longer an empty slogan. AI-related topics and discussions have become the sure-fire “traffic magnet” of the tech world; from autonomous driving to intelligent customer service, every industry seems eager to ride this wave of AI hype.

But as testing professionals, when we face the rapid development of AI, what we care about most is probably this: What can AI actually do in software testing? Can it really help us improve output and efficiency? Or, as it evolves, will AI completely replace testing roles?

In this article, let us explore this topic.

The Role of AI in the Different Stages of Software Testing

AI testing, when it comes down to it, is about having AI take on part of, assist with, or enhance the original testing work. In other words, AI itself does not change the underlying laws of the software testing lifecycle within software development.

Therefore, we can look at what role AI can play from the perspective of the different stages of the software testing lifecycle and the scope of testing responsibilities.

Requirements Analysis Stage

At this stage, we can use AI’s natural language processing technology to sort out the original requirements documents and produce analysis results including business flowcharts, operation flowcharts, and data flow diagrams.

At the same time, we can combine more relevant local data — such as historical bug data, test logs, and project data — to identify testing priorities, build risk models, and detect risks. Based on these analysis results, we can then help formulate a more reasonable test plan.

Test Case Design Stage

During the software design and development phase, testers usually complete test design in parallel. At this stage, we can leverage AI to help us generate test cases based on the requirements documents and the results of the requirements analysis phase. With AI, we can produce more and fuller positive and negative cases as well as a variety of boundary conditions to expand coverage.

Test Preparation Stage

At this stage, the main work is setting up and deploying the test environment. We can use AI capabilities combined with a CI platform to achieve intelligent management of test servers and database environments, as well as the dynamic allocation of resources.

Test Execution Stage

During the execution stage, we can dynamically adjust the test order based on factors such as various risk assessments, dependencies, and business impact, prioritizing coverage of higher-risk modules so as to expose defects as early as possible.

In addition, AI can enhance capabilities such as log analysis and image comparison, improving our test execution efficiency and defect detection ability.

Test Reporting Stage

In the closing part of testing, using AI to perform comprehensive analysis of various process data can help us produce multi-dimensional test reports, providing project decision-makers with a structured analysis of testing status.

How AI Empowers Software Testing at This Stage

The current development of AI can already provide more support in many typical testing scenarios. The following outlines some typical scenarios that can be empowered by AI:

  • Intelligent Data Generation - Create diverse datasets covering common scenarios and edge cases
  • Test Automation - Automatically adapt to UI changes to keep automation scripts stable
  • Precise Regression Testing - Intelligently select related test cases based on code changes
  • Process Cloning - Learn testing workflows and then automatically execute similar processes
  • Dynamic Waiting Mechanism - Intelligently judge page load status before performing actions
  • Intelligent Log Analysis - Analyze and identify potential problem patterns in error logs
  • Load / Performance Testing - Simulate real user behavior and diagnose performance bottlenecks
  • Continuous Test Monitoring - Monitor application status in real time and alert on anomalies
  • Exploratory Testing Support - Provide intelligent suggestions during exploratory testing
  • Predictive Analysis - Predict release risks based on historical data

The Advantages of Introducing AI

AI can keep learning, training, and improving continuously, so after introducing AI, we can build advantages across many of the following aspects:

  • Cost Optimization - Reduce labor costs, optimize resource allocation, and speed up time to market
  • Stable and Reliable - Ensure standardized test execution and result consistency
  • Early Defect Screening - Expose problems early and shorten the fix cycle
  • Fast Feedback - Run tests in parallel across multiple environments to shorten the feedback loop
  • High-Quality Cases - Automatically generate diverse cases such as unit tests, regression tests, and API tests

Significant Challenges Still Remain in Applying AI

Artificial Intelligence or “Artificial Stupidity”?

If AI’s training data is biased, the results can be so absurd that they make you question reality. If the training outcome of AI is not ideal, then applying AI may not only fail to improve efficiency, but also waste a large amount of extra resources correcting its execution results.

Data Dependency Syndrome

AI’s high demands for quality training data and various parameter adjustments often impose significant constraints on real-world deployment in specific industries.

Maintenance Costs Are Higher Than You Think

Beyond the investment in data resources, training models on local datasets also requires a great deal of time and money, including equipment resources, which are a considerable expense. In addition, the current shortage of AI talent makes the labor cost of AI applications much higher.

Experience and Intuition Are Things AI Can Never Learn

Veteran testers with rich experience can sniff out hidden defects in a product from all kinds of subtle clues; this “mystical,” sixth-sense-like ability is bound to be difficult for AI to replicate.

Assistant or Adversary?

“With AI developing like this, are test engineers going to lose their jobs?” There is really no need to panic!

AI is still essentially a tool. Just as test automation replaced some manual checks, it only changes parts of the way we work rather than eliminating the role altogether. Future testers will be more like an “AI Trainer + Strategy Commander” — what we actually need to do boils down to the following:

  • Teach AI to understand business logic (for example, what a “correct order status transition” is);
  • Design smarter testing strategies (for example, how to balance automation and exploratory testing);
  • Interpret AI’s results and make decisions (for example, whether a given anomaly is a bug or a false positive).

AI is like a robotic vacuum: it can help you clean the floor, but when it comes to stubborn stains (complex business scenarios) or changes in furniture layout (requirement changes), you still have to step in yourself.

Conclusion - AI Is Not the End, but a New Starting Point

The application of AI in software testing is still in its infancy. We can see its enormous potential, but it is not yet time to place full trust in it and abandon the original models. As testers, rather than worrying about “whether we will be replaced,” it is better to actively embrace change: learn some basic machine learning, get to know mainstream AI testing tools, and even take part in training your own models.

After all, in the future world of software testing, the most sought-after people will certainly not be “those who are best at clicking a mouse,” but “those who are best at working with AI”. What do you think?

Some earlier articles also discussed the development of AI. For further reading:

In the AI Era, Do Programmers Still Have a Future?

The Testing Profession and Its Future Prospects

With the rapid development of AI technology, from ChatGPT to the explosion of DeepSeek, AI can now genuinely play a role in assisting our daily work.

Beyond specific areas such as assisted programming and copywriting, we can also make full use of AI’s powerful logical capabilities and vast foundational data to help us propose practical and feasible improvement plans for some of the difficulties we encounter at work.

But for AI to give us actionable solutions, the design of the prompt framework and the contextual information provided to AI are extremely critical. A well-designed prompt framework can help us quickly obtain highly valuable references.

A Case of the Predicament We Face

Here we use a fairly common case of an agile team’s quality predicament to illustrate:

As a test engineer responsible for quality assurance in an agile team running the Scrum framework, the team also includes an SM, a PO, two Android developers (among whom Xiao Li is responsible for the overall system design of the App), one back-end developer, and one part-time visual designer. The team’s product is a companion Android App for an IoT smart bracelet product. However, due to issues such as coordination with the hardware team, frequently changing requirements, untimely visual design, delayed test submissions, and a backlog of bugs, product quality is not optimistic. The App has now gone through multiple iterations, and the planned launch date is drawing ever closer. How can we propose an improvement plan for the current quality predicament?

Designing the Prompt Framework

For AI to help us produce a feasible improvement plan, we first need to design the prompt framework reasonably, so that the final plan better fits the team’s current situation and is actionable.

The key points of the prompt framework design are then:

  • A given role, so that AI determines from what perspective to propose the improvement plan
  • The current status quo, that is, sufficient background information and context
  • What AI should analyze in detail, or what its task should be
  • The specific output expected from AI, including format requirements and the elements to be included
  • Some relevant constraints, which have an important impact on whether the plan is feasible

item.title: Why Did DeepSeek Choose Open Source?
item.description:
Someone asked: the major large models abroad are basically all closed source, so why did DeepSeek, being so capable, choose to open source?

To answer this question, you actually only need to understand who Liang Wenfeng is, how he made his start, and a few of his interviews available online, and it becomes clear!

DeepSeek Is a Product of Interest

As one of China’s leading quantitative private funds, High-Flying has dominated the field by relying on AI technologies such as machine learning, and it has already been enormously successful. In other words, High-Flying already earns more than enough money on its own; building the DeepSeek large model on top of its existing technical accumulation is more a product of the founders’ personal interest than a core product. At most, the original intent was to empower its core business—but it was absolutely never its main track.

Of course, now that DeepSeek has reached this position, it is not out of the question that High-Flying’s direction could become large models in the future.

It is just like Nokia originally making pulp, or Lamborghini originally making tractors…. An unintentional result that took root.

So the first consideration in building DeepSeek was not the business model, not how to make money! Whether to open source or stay closed source was not much of a dilemma in terms of business model!

The Core of Technology Is Not the Technology Itself, but the Talent That Produces It

And from Liang Wenfeng’s interviews, we can also learn his view on open source: people are the key to innovation! In the face of a disruptive innovation like AI, the moat gained through closed source is extremely short-lived; it is passionate, curious, daring top talent that is the source of such technology!

He also gave the example of NVIDIA: there is nothing particularly secret about NVIDIA’s technology itself, but assembling a team, building an ecosystem, and catching up all take time—and that time is the real moat!

The confidence in one’s bones and the sense of mission to take the world upon oneself

In his interviews, Liang Wenfeng repeatedly spoke about how China’s earlier technological development was mostly that of a follower, with incremental, fine-tuning innovations but a lack of disruptive innovation. There is a need to move from the imitation stage toward original creation, and to reflect Chinese contributions within the progress of human technology. I believe this is also the result of his giving the all-domestic talent on his team, on the foundation of his financial strength, ample freedom and room to innovate, accumulating strength over time and then breaking through!

Liang Wenfeng has truly lived up to the ideal: when you succeed, help the whole world succeed

item.title: Musk's Audit Storm, an AI Shock More Direct Than DeepSeek
item.description:
During the Spring Festival holiday, everyone here was celebrating in high spirits. The box office of Ne Zha kept climbing; DeepSeek also broke into the mainstream, dominating everyone’s feeds, with its servers busy for long stretches.

At the same time, across the ocean, as Trump moved into the White House on January 20, Musk also took charge of DOGE and got to work at lightning speed that very day, launching a large-scale audit of federal government spending.

This DOGE is not the cryptocurrency DOGE; it is short for the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency.

Musk and the DOGE Audit Storm

Unlike the traditional large-scale audits we might imagine — first setting up an audit department, then hundreds or even thousands of auditors spending months on preparation, on-site work, and reconciliation — DOGE has, in less than 20 days, already turned American politics upside down.

— January 20: shut down the Chief Diversity Officers Executive Council (CDOEC);

— January 25: canceled about $420 million in existing / soon-to-be-signed contracts;

— January 27: the Departments of Labor, Transportation, Agriculture, Commerce, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury canceled 16 DEIA contracts, saving $145 million;

— January 28: the General Services Administration (GSA) terminated three leases on nearly empty office space and shut down 17 DEIA websites, saving $1.6 million;

— January 29: canceled a $45 million DEI scholarship for Myanmar;

(As of January 29, 2025, 26 departments including the Department of Education and the GSA had terminated 85 DEIA-related contracts totaling about $1 billion;)

— February 3: the number of terminated leases on underutilized buildings rose to 22, and the savings grew from $1.6 million to $44.6 million;

— February 3: shut down the United States Agency for International Development (USAID);

— February 4: six agencies terminated 36 contracts, saving about $165 million in total, including the Department of Homeland Security’s “Humanities Research and Climate Support Services” contract;

— February 5: terminated 12 consulting contracts (at the GSA and the Department of Education), saving about $30 million in total;

— February 6: the Social Security Administration terminated its “Gender X Initiative Marker” contract, saving over $1 million; NASA canceled its Politico subscription, saving $500,000; 78 contracts in the DEI, distressed assets, media, and consulting categories were terminated, for total savings of about $110 million;

— February 8: announced that within the past 48 hours, the Department of Health and Human Services had canceled 62 contracts worth $182 million; the Department of Education terminated three DEI training grants totaling $15 million.

Yet behind such fast and efficient audit results and actions there is no massive team — it relies on nothing more than a few geniuses barely in their twenties, backed by their AI algorithms.

DOGE’s Six Young Prodigies

Hard to imagine, but every move on the list above was carried out by the six young men below.

  • Gavin Kliger (25): A graduate of UC Berkeley in electrical engineering and computer science, Kliger was formerly a senior software engineer at the U.S. AI data analytics company Databricks and is an expert in artificial intelligence and big data analysis. His job is to draft executive orders and ensure they take effect quickly within the government — the email telling all USAID staff they need not return to headquarters on Monday came from his hand. He also directly drafted the funding review order targeting the U.S. Treasury, took part in OPM’s mass layoff plan, and was responsible for setting the “rehire standards” for civil servants, requiring that future government employees be approved by DOGE before being hired.

  • Luke Farritor (23): Farritor dropped out of the University of Nebraska–Lincoln and later worked for Nat Friedman, the Silicon Valley entrepreneur behind GitHub. He once interned at SpaceX, writing software for the pumps, valves, and other components that help fuel rockets. Farritor is currently listed as an “executive engineer” in the office of the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), and personally oversaw the digital lockdown operation at USAID; his next target is already the systems of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which handles contracts.

  • Edward Coristine (19): The youngest of the group, Coristine had just graduated from high school and was studying mechanical engineering and physics at Northeastern University in Boston. He spent three months last summer working at Musk’s brain-computer interface company Neuralink, and his specific duties have not yet been made clear. Coristine once joined a call with U.S. General Services Administration employees using a non-government Google Gmail account, asking them to review code he had written and justify their own work — a move that sparked dissatisfaction among federal employees.

  • Akash Bobba (21): Bobba comes from UC Berkeley and was an investment engineering intern at Bridgewater Associates; he had also interned at Meta and at Palantir, the U.S. software services company founded by MAGA backer Peter Thiel. He specializes in artificial intelligence, data analysis, and financial modeling. He is responsible for designing algorithms to monitor the flow of government funds, leading a “real-time fiscal spending monitoring system” that allows federal “inefficient spending” to be frozen in real time without congressional review.

  • Ethan Shaotran (22): A senior computer science major at Harvard, Shaotran is the only one on the team with AI startup experience. The AI company he founded, Energize AI, received $100,000 in funding from OpenAI, and he once took second place in a hackathon held by Musk’s AI company xAI. Shaotran leads DOGE’s AI government initiative, whose goal is to replace the government’s traditional human decision-making with algorithms, automating most administrative approvals, budget evaluations, and even congressional reports.

  • Gautier Cole Killian (24): Breached the Treasury’s security systems and obtained access to the payment network. A graduate of McGill University, Killian is exceptionally strong in financial data processing and once worked as an engineer at Jump Trading, a firm specializing in high-frequency financial trading and algorithms. His main task is to help the DOGE team break through the Treasury’s security defenses, giving them access to the government payment network and letting them bypass security checks to read millions of transaction records directly. Killian is also one of the few young people granted senior White House access, and Musk places extremely high trust in him.

So these few engineers, barely out of college, after obtaining data access and in only about two weeks, used AI to bring to the surface all sorts of problems that had lain hidden beneath the iceberg for decades. You could say it truly was a case of speed being everything — the bureaucrats over in the U.S. probably hadn’t even come to their senses before finding their house had been raided.

Reflections

No matter where this reform storm ultimately takes Musk and his six young lieutenants, AI has already, in a jaw-dropping way, begun to sway the political situation across the ocean, and it is bound to deeply affect every aspect of our lives.
